question: With no internal documents to hand, an analyst asks Claude to list the standard requirements for a customer complaints process and pastes the reply straight into the project brief. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The analyst will have to repeat the request if the conversation is closed before the reply is saved.
B) The brief will be rather longer than the sponsor expects and may need trimming before the next review meeting.
C) The brief will carry generic requirements that sound authoritative but reflect no source and no context.
D) The reply may be phrased for a general audience rather than in the complaints team's own vocabulary.
correct_answers: C) The brief will carry generic requirements that sound authoritative but reflect no source and no context.
explanations: Losing the reply costs a few minutes to regenerate. It is an inconvenience rather than a risk to the correctness of the requirements the project will be run against.

Length is easy to fix and easy to notice. A brief that is too long gets edited, whereas plausible requirements nobody sourced tend to survive review precisely because they read like standard practice.

Correct. Asked for standard requirements with no material to work from, Claude produces a confident generic list. Pasted straight into the brief it becomes the team's stated scope, even though it reflects no regulator, no system and no customer this organisation actually has.
Vocabulary mismatch is a readability problem that a rewrite fixes. It may slow the team down slightly, but the brief would still be built on requirements that were never traced to anything real.
